parsed_answer.content:
Method-level security in Spring Security is a declarative mechanism that enforces authorization constraints directly on service or controller methods, rather than relying solely on URL-based filtering. It operates by leveraging Spring AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) to intercept method invocations. When a method annotated with security constraints is called, a proxy—typically a CGLIB or JDK dynamic proxy—intercepts the call, evaluates the security expression, and either proceeds to the target method or throws an AccessDeniedException. This approach is superior to URL-based security for complex domain logic because it is decoupled from the web layer, allowing you to protect business logic even when invoked from non-HTTP sources like scheduled tasks, message listeners, or internal service-to-service calls.

@Secured is the legacy, role-based annotation. It is simple, fast, and strictly evaluates whether the authenticated principal possesses one of the specified authorities (e.g., 'ROLE_ADMIN'). It does not support SpEL (Spring Expression Language), making it rigid but highly performant. In contrast, @PreAuthorize is the modern, flexible standard. It evaluates SpEL expressions, allowing for dynamic, context-aware authorization. With @PreAuthorize, you can reference method arguments (e.g., #id), perform logical combinations (AND/OR), or even call custom beans to determine access, providing a fine-grained 'ABAC' (Attribute-Based Access Control) capability that @Secured simply cannot match.

items: Method security requires @EnableMethodSecurity (or @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in older versions) to register the MethodSecurityInterceptor in the Spring context.
The interceptor is applied via AOP proxies. If you call a secured method from within the same class (self-invocation), the proxy is bypassed, and security checks will not trigger.
@PreAuthorize is evaluated before the method body executes, while @PostAuthorize is evaluated after, allowing you to filter or verify the return value of the method.
SpEL expressions in @PreAuthorize can invoke any bean in the ApplicationContext using the '@beanName.method()' syntax, enabling complex external authorization lookups.

parsed_answer.content: A common 'gotcha' for senior engineers is the self-invocation trap. Because Spring AOP uses proxies, calling a method annotated with @PreAuthorize from another method within the same bean will bypass the security interceptor entirely. If you must have internal calls secured, you should either refactor the secured method into a separate component or inject the bean into itself (using @Lazy to avoid circular dependencies) to force the call through the proxy.
